concept: On the space station gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are falling together, moving sideways so fast (about 28,000 km/h) that they keep missing Earth.

misconceptions.label: There's (almost) no gravity up there
misconceptions.why_tempting: Floating astronauts look exactly like gravity has been switched off.
misconceptions.refutation: About 400 km up, Earth's gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. That pull is what keeps the station going around Earth instead of flying off.
misconceptions.source_note: NASA: 'Some people think that there is no gravity in space' ... at the station's altitude 'Earth's gravity is about 90 percent of what it is on the planet's surface'

misconceptions.label: Gravity doesn't weaken with height
misconceptions.why_tempting: We never feel gravity change in daily life, so it seems the same everywhere.
misconceptions.refutation: Gravity weakens with distance from Earth's center. 400 km up you're about 6% farther from the center, so the pull is about 89% of ground level.
misconceptions.source_note: 'Gravity decreases with altitude as one rises above the Earth's surface because greater altitude means greater distance from the Earth's centre'

misconceptions.label: Orbiting isn't falling
misconceptions.why_tempting: The station never gets closer to the ground, so it doesn't look like it's falling.
misconceptions.refutation: An orbit is a fall that keeps missing: the station falls toward Earth nonstop but moves sideways so fast the ground curves away. You and the ball fall with it, so nothing drops to the floor.
misconceptions.source_note: NASA: 'why do astronauts float there? The answer is because they are in free fall'

misconceptions.label: Staying up is about being high
misconceptions.why_tempting: Space starts only about 100 km up, so it seems the hard part is climbing high enough.
misconceptions.refutation: The hard part is speed: to keep missing Earth, the station has to move sideways at about 28,000 km/h, roughly 30 times as fast as an airliner.
misconceptions.source_note: Munroe, What If 'Orbital Speed': 'The reason it's hard to get to orbit isn't that space is high up. It's hard ... because you have to go so fast'

items.prompt: The International Space Station circles Earth about 400 km up, where astronauts float. Up there, how strong is Earth's gravity compared with on the ground?
An astronaut on the space station lets go of a ball. It hangs in the air next to her instead of dropping to the floor. Why?

options.text: Earth's pull is too weak that high up to notice
The ball, the astronaut and the station are all falling around Earth together, so the ball never gets closer to the floor

steps: Gravity pulls the station, the astronaut and the ball toward Earth, at almost the same strength as on the ground.
All three are moving sideways at the same speed, so all three fall along the same curved path.
Falling together, nothing presses on the floor and nothing gets closer to it.
That's 'weightlessness': not missing gravity, but falling freely with your surroundings.

items.prompt: To stay in orbit about 400 km up, how fast does the space station have to move sideways? (A jet airliner flies about 900 km/h.)

options.text: About jet speed: once it's high enough, it just has to keep moving
It doesn't need sideways speed: it's above most of Earth's pull
About 30 times as fast as a jet
